prompt: What does the first Hohenberg-Kohn theorem say about the ground-state density?

options.text: It fixes the external potential, up to an added constant, and so every property of the system
options.why: Different potentials (beyond a constant) cannot share one ground-state density, so the density identifies the system.

options.text: It is equal to the square of a single electron wavefunction
options.why: Tempting from the one-electron case, but for many electrons the density sums over all of them.

options.text: It can be computed without knowing anything about the system
options.why: Tempting because the theorem sounds general, but it says the density carries the information, not that it is free.

hints: Think about what the density lab in module 3 recovered from a density.
The theorem works backwards: from the result to the potential that caused it.

prompt: What does the second Hohenberg-Kohn theorem give you?

options.text: A way to find the ground state: the true density gives the lowest value of the energy functional
options.why: This turns the problem into a search for the density with the lowest energy.

options.text: The exact formula for the energy functional
options.why: Tempting, but the theorem proves the functional exists without giving it.

options.text: The energies of all excited states
options.why: Tempting from "every property", but the variational statement is about the ground state.

hints: It is a variational principle.
Variational means the right answer is the lowest one.

prompt: Which statements about the Hohenberg-Kohn theorems are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: They apply to the ground state
options.why: Both statements are about the lowest-energy state.

options.text: They prove that an energy functional of the density exists
options.why: Existence is proved; the form is not given.

options.text: They tell us the exact exchange-correlation functional
options.why: Tempting, but that remains unknown and must be approximated.

options.text: They guarantee that an approximate DFT energy is above the true energy
options.why: Tempting from the variational principle, but that holds for the exact functional only.

hints: Separate what is proved from what is computed.
Ask whether each statement needs the functional's formula.

prompt: Two calculations of the same molecule differ only by a constant added to the external potential everywhere. What happens to the ground-state density?

options.text: It is the same
options.why: A constant shifts every energy equally and changes no wavefunction or density; that is why the theorem says "up to a constant".

options.text: It moves towards the higher potential
options.why: Tempting because forces come from potentials, but a constant has no slope, so there is no force.

options.text: It shrinks
options.why: Tempting, but nothing about the shape of the potential changed.

hints: A constant potential has no gradient.
The density lab in module 3 showed the potential only up to a constant.

prompt: Why do the Hohenberg-Kohn theorems not directly give you the band gap?

options.text: The gap involves excited states, while the theorems concern the ground state
options.why: Adding or removing electrons goes beyond the ground state of the original system.

options.text: Because band gaps do not depend on the density
options.why: Tempting, but the gap does depend on the electrons; the issue is which state the theorems cover.

options.text: Because the theorems only work for molecules
options.why: Tempting, but they apply to any system of electrons in an external potential, including crystals.

hints: Which state do the theorems talk about?
A gap compares states with different numbers of electrons or excitations.

prompt: What is the Kohn-Sham system?

options.text: Non-interacting electrons in an effective potential chosen so that they have the real density
options.why: The stand-ins are easy to solve and reproduce the density, which is all the theorems need.

options.text: The real electrons with their repulsion switched off
options.why: Tempting, but switching off repulsion without changing the potential gives the wrong density.

options.text: A model where every electron sits on its own atom
options.why: Tempting from chemistry pictures, but Kohn-Sham orbitals can spread over the whole crystal.

hints: The key word is "same density".
Think of a flight simulator tuned to respond like the real plane.

prompt: Which part of the energy does the Kohn-Sham trick compute exactly that was hard to get from the density alone?

options.text: Most of the kinetic energy, from the orbitals of the non-interacting electrons
options.why: T_s is computed exactly from the orbitals; only a small remainder goes into exchange-correlation.

options.text: The attraction to the nuclei
options.why: Tempting, but that was already easy: it is an integral of the density times the potential.

options.text: The exchange-correlation energy
options.why: Tempting, but that is exactly the part still left to approximate.

hints: Which energy term caused trouble for density-only theories?
Orbitals are needed to compute this term well.

prompt: Which are true of Kohn-Sham orbitals? Select all that apply.

options.text: Filling them gives the density
options.why: n is the sum of the occupations times the squared orbitals.

options.text: Each holds up to two electrons, one of each spin
options.why: As for any spatial orbital under the Pauli principle.

options.text: They are the exact many-electron wavefunction
options.why: Tempting, but they belong to the stand-in system.

options.text: Their energies are routinely used as band energies
options.why: They are auxiliary, but in practice they are read as bands, with known caveats for the gap.

hints: They belong to a helper system.
Think about how the density is assembled.

prompt: Where does the approximation enter in Kohn-Sham DFT?

options.text: Only in the exchange-correlation functional
options.why: The construction is exact in principle; everything unknown is collected into E_xc.

options.text: In replacing interacting by non-interacting electrons
options.why: Tempting, but this replacement is exact by construction because the potential is tuned.

options.text: In using the density instead of the wavefunction
options.why: Tempting, but the Hohenberg-Kohn theorems make that exact for the ground state.

hints: Which piece is unknown?
The theory is exact in principle until you pick a functional.

prompt: What is the Hartree potential?

options.text: The classical electrostatic repulsion from the whole electron density
options.why: It treats the density as a smooth cloud of charge.

options.text: The attraction of the electrons to the nuclei
options.why: Tempting, but that is the external potential.

options.text: The quantum effect that keeps same-spin electrons apart
options.why: Tempting, but that is exchange, which sits in the exchange-correlation term.

hints: Hartree is the classical piece.
Think of a charged fog.

prompt: Why does the Hartree potential contain a self-interaction error?

options.text: Each electron is part of the density, so it is counted as repelling its own charge
options.why: The exact theory removes this; exchange-correlation approximations do so only partly.

options.text: Because it ignores the nuclei
options.why: Tempting, but the nuclei are in the external potential, not the Hartree term.

options.text: Because it uses the wrong value of the electron charge
options.why: Tempting, but the charge is exact; the problem is which charges are counted.

hints: What does an electron "see" in the Hartree potential?
The density includes every electron.

prompt: In the lab's two-electron closed-shell model, what fraction of the Hartree potential enters the Fock operator?

options.text: One half: exchange cancels the other half
options.why: For two electrons in one spatial orbital the exchange term equals minus half the Hartree term.

options.text: All of it
options.why: Tempting, but that would leave each electron repelling itself fully.

options.text: None of it
options.why: Tempting, but then the electrons would not repel each other at all.

hints: Exchange removes self-interaction exactly in Hartree-Fock.
With two electrons in one orbital, half the cloud is the electron itself.

prompt: In the SCF lab you switch the repulsion off. Why does the loop then converge in a single step?

options.text: The potential no longer depends on the density, so the first solution is already self-consistent
options.why: Without the Hartree term, nothing feeds back from the density into the potential.

options.text: Because the mixing becomes 1
options.why: Tempting, but the mixing slider is unchanged; there is simply nothing left to iterate.

options.text: Because the density becomes zero
options.why: Tempting, but there are still two electrons and a density that integrates to 2.

hints: What links the density back to the potential?
Remove the link and the loop has nothing to chase.

prompt: Which effects does the exchange-correlation term account for?

options.text: The Pauli avoidance of same-spin electrons, the extra dodging due to repulsion, and the kinetic-energy remainder
options.why: E_xc is defined as everything not in T_s, the external energy and the Hartree energy.

options.text: The attraction to the nuclei
options.why: Tempting, but that is known exactly as the external potential.

options.text: Only the classical repulsion of the charge cloud
options.why: Tempting, but that is the Hartree term.

hints: It is the leftover piece.
Exchange plus correlation plus a little kinetic energy.

prompt: Put these functional families in order from the lowest rung of Jacob's ladder to the highest.

options.text: LDA (local density)
options.why: Uses only the density at each point.

options.text: GGA, such as PBE
options.why: Adds the gradient of the density.

options.text: Meta-GGA, such as r2SCAN
options.why: Adds the kinetic-energy density.

options.text: Hybrid, such as HSE06
options.why: Mixes in a fraction of exact exchange.

hints: Each rung adds an ingredient.
Cost usually rises as you climb.

prompt: What does VASP use for exchange-correlation if the INCAR says nothing about it?

options.text: The functional named in the POTCAR files, PBE for the standard PAW sets
options.why: VASP reads the default from the POTCAR (VASP wiki page GGA).

options.text: LDA always
options.why: Tempting because LDA is the simplest, but the POTCAR decides.

options.text: A hybrid functional
options.why: Tempting because hybrids are accurate, but they must be requested and are much more expensive.

hints: Look at what the POTCAR carries.
The common POTCAR sets were generated with PBE.

prompt: Why is the exchange-correlation functional the place where DFT results differ between studies?

options.text: It is the only approximated part, so different choices give different errors
options.why: Everything else is exact in principle; the functional decides the systematic error.

options.text: Because the Hartree potential is approximated differently in each code
options.why: Tempting, but the Hartree term is exact for a given density.

options.text: Because the Hohenberg-Kohn theorems are only approximate
options.why: Tempting, but they are exact theorems.

hints: Which piece is a model, not a theorem?
Two careful studies with different functionals can disagree.

prompt: Which three parts make up the Kohn-Sham effective potential?

options.text: External (nuclei), Hartree and exchange-correlation
options.why: v_eff = v_ext + v_H + v_xc.

options.text: Kinetic, potential and total
options.why: Tempting from mechanics, but kinetic energy is an operator in the equation, not part of the potential.

options.text: Core, valence and vacuum
options.why: Tempting from VASP vocabulary, but these are regions or electron groups, not potential terms.

hints: One is from the nuclei, two from the electrons.
Two parts are known exactly.

prompt: Which parts of the effective potential change when the density changes? Select all that apply.

options.text: The Hartree potential
options.why: It is computed from the density.

options.text: The exchange-correlation potential
options.why: It is a functional derivative of E_xc, evaluated at the density.

options.text: The external potential from fixed nuclei
options.why: Tempting, but with the nuclei held still it does not depend on the electrons.

hints: Which parts are built from the electrons?
The nuclei do not move during the electronic loop.

prompt: Why does a density-dependent effective potential force an iterative solution?

options.text: You need the potential to get the orbitals, and the orbitals to get the density that defines the potential
options.why: The equations are coupled, so you guess and improve until they agree.

options.text: Because computers cannot solve eigenvalue problems directly
options.why: Tempting, but each individual eigenvalue problem is solved; the coupling is the issue.

options.text: Because the nuclei move during the calculation
options.why: Tempting, but even with fixed nuclei the loop is needed.

hints: Draw the circle: potential, orbitals, density.
Where does the circle close?

prompt: In the SCF lab, the effective potential (solid line) lies above the nuclear potential (dashed). Why?

options.text: The added Hartree repulsion is positive, so it raises the potential where the electrons are
options.why: Repulsion pushes the potential up; in the lab half of v_H is added.

options.text: Because the nuclear charge is reduced during the loop
options.why: Tempting, but Z is fixed by the selector.

options.text: Because of a plotting offset
options.why: Tempting, but both curves share the same axis and offset.

hints: What sign does repulsion have?
The difference between the curves is v_H / 2.

prompt: Put the steps of one SCF iteration in order.

options.text: Start from an input density
options.why: A guess at first, the mixed density later.

options.text: Build the effective potential
options.why: Hartree and exchange-correlation from the density.

options.text: Solve for the orbitals
options.why: The one-electron equations in that potential.

options.text: Compute the output density
options.why: Fill the orbitals and add them up.

options.text: Mix and check the change
options.why: Mix input and output, and stop if the change is small enough.

hints: The potential comes from the density.
Checking is the last step before going round again.

prompt: What does "self-consistent" mean?

options.text: The output density equals the input density: the density reproduces itself
options.why: Then the potential, orbitals and density all agree.

options.text: The energy is the lowest possible for any functional
options.why: Tempting, but self-consistency is about agreement within one functional.

options.text: The calculation gives the same answer on every computer
options.why: Tempting from the word "consistent", but it is about the loop.

hints: Compare what goes in with what comes out.
A fixed point does not change when you apply the loop again.

prompt: In VASP, what decides when the electronic loop stops?

options.text: EDIFF: the energy change between steps falls below it, or NELM steps are reached
options.why: EDIFF is the tolerance and NELM the ceiling (VASP wiki pages EDIFF and NELM).

options.text: EDIFFG
options.why: Tempting because it looks similar, but EDIFFG controls the ionic relaxation.

options.text: ENCUT
options.why: Tempting because it controls accuracy, but it sets the basis size, not the loop.

hints: One tag is a tolerance, one a ceiling.
The G in EDIFFG stands for geometry.

prompt: The VASP default electronic tolerance EDIFF is 1E-4 eV. Your protocol uses 1E-6. By what factor is the protocol tighter?
hints: Divide the default by the tighter value.
1E-4 divided by 1E-6.

prompt: Your run printed 60 electronic steps for one ionic step and moved on. What should you conclude?

options.text: That step probably hit NELM without converging, so its energy and forces are unreliable
options.why: 60 is the default NELM; VASP continues without an error message.

options.text: It converged, because VASP would stop otherwise
options.why: Tempting, but VASP does not stop when NELM is reached.

options.text: The structure is wrong
options.why: Tempting, but many causes are possible; first check the electronic convergence.

hints: What is the default NELM?
Does VASP stop with an error at NELM?

prompt: Why mix the new density with the old one instead of taking the new one directly?

options.text: Taking the full new density often overshoots and oscillates; mixing damps the swing
options.why: A fraction of the change is a smaller, steadier step.

options.text: To save memory
options.why: Tempting, but mixing usually needs more memory (the history of densities).

options.text: Because the new density is always wrong
options.why: Tempting, but it is a better estimate; the issue is overcorrection.

hints: Think of steering too hard.
The lab at alpha = 1 for Z = 1 shows what happens.

prompt: In the SCF lab you lower alpha from 0.3 to 0.05. What do you expect?

options.text: The loop still converges but needs many more iterations
options.why: Smaller steps are safe but slow; the residual line on the log plot becomes shallower.

options.text: It diverges
options.why: Tempting, but small steps are the safe direction.

options.text: It converges in fewer iterations
options.why: Tempting, but each step now removes only a small part of the error.

hints: Small steps are stable.
How much of the error does each step remove?

prompt: With linear mixing, the new input density is (1 - alpha) n_in + alpha n_out. If alpha = 0.3, n_in = 1.0 and n_out = 2.0 at a point, what is the new input density there?
hints: Take 70 % of the old value and 30 % of the new one.
0.7 times 1.0 plus 0.3 times 2.0.

prompt: What are the VASP defaults for AMIX and BMIX?

options.why: From the VASP wiki pages AMIX and BMIX, as summarised in the author's handbook.
Tempting, but 0.0001 is the BMIX value used to approximate linear mixing in difficult cases.
Tempting, but these are the damped values for stubborn systems, not the defaults.

hints: The defaults are moderate.
The damped values come from the troubleshooting ladder.

prompt: The energy in OSZICAR jumps up and down from step to step in a metal slab. What is the likely cause?

options.text: Charge sloshing: the mixer overcorrects long-range charge movements
options.why: Metals and slabs respond strongly at long wavelength.

options.text: ENCUT is too high
options.why: Tempting, but a higher cutoff gives a better basis, not oscillation.

options.text: The k-mesh is too dense
options.why: Tempting, but a denser mesh improves sampling; it does not cause oscillation.

hints: Think of the lab at alpha = 1.
Which systems move charge over long distances cheaply?

prompt: What is the first thing to change for charge sloshing?

options.text: Lower AMIX and BMIX step by step
options.why: Smaller mixing damps the swing, which is the cause.

options.text: Raise NELM to 500
options.why: Tempting, but more steps of an oscillating loop rarely converge.

options.text: Lower EDIFF
options.why: Tempting because it sounds stricter, but it makes convergence harder, not easier.

hints: Fix the cause, not the symptom.
Mixing is what overshoots.

prompt: Order these actions for a loop that will not converge, from first to last.

options.text: Check the structure and inputs are sensible
options.why: A bad structure cannot be fixed by mixing.

options.text: Change the mixing (AMIX, BMIX)
options.why: This addresses the most common cause.

options.text: Try a more robust algorithm (ALGO = All or Damped)
options.why: For stalling and difficult magnetic or +U systems.

options.text: Raise NELM
options.why: Only once the loop is heading the right way.

hints: Start with the cheapest and most fundamental checks.
Raising the ceiling comes last.

prompt: Which tricks give a difficult loop a better starting point? Select all that apply.

options.text: Converge without spin first, then restart spin-polarized from the CHGCAR
options.why: A good starting density helps the magnetic loop.

options.text: Converge with a larger SIGMA, then restart with the small one
options.why: Smearing smooths the occupations at first.

options.text: Delete the WAVECAR and CHGCAR before every restart
options.why: Tempting as a clean start, but it throws away the good starting point.

options.text: Raise NELMDL so the orbitals settle before the density is updated
options.why: More non-self-consistent warm-up steps help a wild start.

hints: A good start is a density close to the answer.
Which options reuse earlier work?

prompt: With linear mixing and an error amplification factor lambda, the error is multiplied each step by 1 - alpha (1 - lambda). For lambda = -3, which alpha converges?

options.why: 1 - 0.4 * 4 = -0.6, magnitude below 1, so the error shrinks while flipping sign.
1 - 0.6 * 4 = -1.4, magnitude above 1: the error grows and oscillates.
1 - 4 = -3: the error triples each step, with alternating sign.

hints: Compute 1 - alpha * 4 for each option.
Convergence needs a magnitude below 1.
